## Experiment

Same as `coop --git` with 250 steps (compaction at 28K), but without the shared git remote: the two agents can only message each other. Tests how much the shared remote matters.

## Results

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Setting | `coop`, 2 agents per pair |
| Model | `gemini/gemini-3.8-flash`, high thinking |
| Subset | `flash_10` (10 pairs) |
| Step limit | 250 per agent |
| Compaction | at 28K tokens |
| Passed | 8/10 (80%) |
| Agents stopped at the step limit | 3 |
| Merge conflicts | 0 |
| Agent errors | 0 |
| Cost | `$23.05` (`$2.30` per pair) |
| Wall time | 138 min |

## Observations

- 8/10, the same score and the same two failures as with the shared remote, so the remote made no difference here.
- No merge conflicts, even though agents could not see each other's branches. Agents sent 30 to 78 messages per passing pair. In `typst_task/6554` they exchanged code over messages and submitted identical patches.
- `pallets_jinja_task/1559`: both agents were stopped at step 250 with nothing pushed, and they sent only 3 messages in total. `pillow_task/290`: both agents submitted and the patches merged cleanly, but feature 4 failed 1 of its 8 tests while feature 5 passed all 9.
- Running 10 agents at once hit the API rate limit often (48 retries). This slowed agents and is why we now run about 8 agents per key (see [model_config.md](../../notes/model_config.md)).
